title: the words, line by line, from Luke
hookLine: the words, line by line, from Luke

lines: ONE LONG WORD AT A WAKE.
cards: At a wake, a room full of voices runs it together until it sounds like one long word. A kid in Catholic school rattles it off before anyone can blink.
In football, a desperate pass thrown deep with no time left still gets called a Hail Mary. Said that fast, it's easy to miss where the words came from. Half the prayer isn't new at all.
It's lifted, line by line, from the first chapter of Luke's Gospel. Today, slowly.

teach.b: The first line belongs to an angel: yesterday's Gabriel, in the room in Nazareth. In the Douay-Rheims Bible, his first words are: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women."
Hail is just an old hello. Full of grace is day eight's word, filled to the brim. The next line belongs to a relative.
A little later in Luke, Mary visits her cousin Elizabeth, who's also pregnant, and Elizabeth cries out: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb."

Over the centuries Christians put those two greetings side by side, an angel's and a cousin's, and added two names: Mary, right after the angel's hail, and Jesus at the end. That's the whole first half.
Every word of it, apart from those two names, is from Luke.
Then the prayer turns. The second half isn't scripture.

teach.h: PRAY FOR US, NOW AND AT THE END.
teach.b: It's the Church speaking, and it came into the prayer later: Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen. Listen to the shape.
The first half says hello. The second half asks for something, small and huge at once: pray for us. Now, and at the very end.
Catholics aren't asking Mary to do what only God does. They're asking her to pray with them.
On the rosary it comes ten times in each decade, a greeting, then a request, like a heartbeat. Say it fast and it's a blur. Say it slowly and you're standing in two rooms in Luke's Gospel.

how: Catholics say the Hail Mary ten times on each decade of the rosary, and on its own at many moments of the day; its first half comes from Luke 1:28 and 1:42.

games.q: who said it first — tap the pairs.
p: blessed is the fruit of thy womb

games.q: Mary, newly pregnant, walks into her cousin Elizabeth's house. what does Elizabeth say?
games.why: "blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." her words became the second line of the Hail Mary.

practice: Here's the practice. Let your breath slow down. On the breath in, think of a greeting: hello to someone you love.
On the breath out, think of a request: one thing you need right now. In, a greeting. Out, a request.
If you pray the Hail Mary, you can say it once, as slowly as you've ever said it.

wordCard.voice: The Hail Mary. An angel's hello and a cousin's blessing from Luke, then the Church's request: pray for us. Tenth word.

orig.note: Latin: hail Mary, full of grace. the opening of the prayer in the Church's old language.

carryVoice: Your line: a greeting, then a request. Two rooms in Luke, ten times a decade. Day ten.
